note: Curated MCP stack. `run` entries are provisioned automatically through a package runner; `manual` entries are staged with their prerequisite check because they need a licensed binary, a running app or a database.

servers.name: REA
servers.reason: 229-tool reverse engineering surface: binaries, .NET, Electron, Android, firmware.

servers.name: Context7
servers.reason: Current library and API documentation, so exploits are not written against a hallucinated version.

servers.name: re-mcp (Ghidra)
servers.reason: IDA and Ghidra behind one interface, with meta-tools for the long tail. Needs Ghidra installed and GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR set.

servers.name: ReVa (Ghidra)
servers.manual: Ghidra extension: install the release zip from the repo through Ghidra's File > Install Extensions, then add the MCP command it prints.
servers.reason: LLM-first Ghidra tools with context-rot control; best for long firmware sessions.

servers.name: Burp (official MCP)
servers.manual: Burp Suite: install the official MCP extension from the BApp Store, start Burp, then point OpenHack at the local endpoint it announces.
servers.reason: Proxy history, Repeater, Intruder, scanner and Collaborator (out-of-band callbacks).

servers.name: burp-mcp (61 tools)
servers.manual: Alternative to the official bridge: install the Java extension into Burp Pro and run the Python server. Collaborator polling is the reason to prefer this one for blind bugs.
servers.reason: 61 tools including Collaborator generate/poll, decoder, comparer and Intruder results.

servers.name: HexStrike AI
servers.manual: Clone the repo and run its MCP server with the path to hexstrike_mcp.py; it expects its own tool bundle on the same host.
servers.reason: 150+ security tools behind one door; breadth when a target is unfamiliar.

servers.name: jadx MCP
servers.manual: Install the jadx plugin from the repo, open the APK in jadx, then add the HTTP MCP endpoint it exposes.
servers.reason: Android decompilation and manifest inspection for mobile bounty targets.
